title: Follow that man
hook: Zeno asks the bookseller where men like Socrates can be found, and Crates the Cynic walks past

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zeno's shipwreck: a fortune lost at sea, and a bookshop. Your line was I sailed well when I was wrecked. Did you remember a loss that sent you somewhere good? Day twenty-six.
screen: `ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.`

segments.voice: We left Zeno in a bookshop in Athens, broke, shipwrecked, and completely hooked on a book about Socrates. But Socrates had been dead for generations. So Zeno looks up from the page and asks the bookseller a question. Where can I find men like this? Real ones. Alive. And right at that moment, as if the story had been waiting for its cue, a strange figure walks past the shop door. And the bookseller points at him and says three words. Follow that man.
screen: `SOCRATES WAS LONG DEAD.` → `WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THIS?` → `A STRANGE FIGURE WALKS PAST.`

segments.voice: The man walking past was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. The Cynics were the punk rockers of ancient Greece. They owned almost nothing, slept in public, said exactly what they thought, and mocked anything fake. The name comes from the Greek for dog-like, because they lived as openly as dogs. Crates had been born rich, in Thebes, and given his wealth away. Ancient writers say people called him the door-opener, because he walked into any house he liked and gave the family advice, and they were glad to see him. A woman named Hipparchia, from a wealthy family, fell in love with him and chose his life of the road over her comfortable one, and became a philosopher in her own right. So Zeno followed. He became Crates's student. But there was a problem. Zeno was shy, and the Cynics were shameless on purpose. So Diogenes Laërtius tells this story. Crates hands Zeno a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through a busy part of Athens. Zeno, embarrassed, tries to hide it under his cloak. Crates cracks the pot with his staff. Soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno runs. And Crates calls after him, roughly: why are you running, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Embarrassment, Crates was saying, isn't harm. But look at how it all began. A curious question, asked out loud. A stranger walking past. And the nerve to get up from a bookseller's bench and follow him out the door.
screen: `THE CYNICS: DOG-LIKE, AND PROUD.` · `CRATES, THE DOOR-OPENER.` · `A POT OF LENTIL SOUP.` · `EMBARRASSMENT ISN'T HARM.` · then, large: `FOLLOW THAT MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask yourself Zeno's question, in your own words: where can I find more of this? Something you've been curious about lately, a subject, a skill, a kind of person you'd like to learn from. Let it come. Then picture the bookseller pointing. Where's the door? Who's walking past? A book, a class, a person you could ask. Just notice where the finger points. The bell holds the time.
Follow that man. A bookseller points, a Cynic walks by, and a shipwrecked merchant gets up and follows.
Your line: follow that man. Today, give one curiosity five full minutes. Look it up, ask someone, open the book. Follow it. Day twenty-six.

howItsDone: In the ancient schools, people learned philosophy by attaching themselves to a living teacher and following them about; many people today still seek out a teacher or a community to learn from in person.

fork.setup: you're Crates. your shy new student is hiding a pot of lentil soup under his cloak as you cross a crowded street. what do you do?
options: let him hide it. he'll learn in time.
crack the pot with your staff.
take the pot and carry it yourself.
fork.reveal: Crates breaks the pot, the soup runs down Zeno's legs, Zeno runs, and Crates calls: nothing terrible has happened to you.

original.note: Greek, kynikos: dog-like, from kyon, dog. The name of the Cynic philosophers, and the root of English cynic.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bookseller's throwaway line.
what it means: a curious question asked out loud, and the nerve to get up and follow the answer.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 7.2–3 gives the bookshop and the soup; 6.86 calls Crates the door-opener, and 6.96–98 tells of Hipparchia.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.2–3 (the bookshop; the lentil soup)

notes: Socrates died 399 BCE; Zeno arrived in Athens c. 312 BCE, so the script says 'nearly ninety years'. Confirm Zeno's arrival date.
The soup story (DL 7.3): Crates breaks the pot with his staff; 'Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has befallen you.' Paraphrased.
'Punk rockers of ancient Greece' is a modern analogy; a Keeper may prefer something else.

Review 2026-10-01: cut 'nearly ninety years' (not in Diogenes Laërtius) in the voice and screen; the unsourced claim that the soup lesson 'stayed with Zeno for life' and the stock ending 'a lot of great lives start just like that' replaced with a concrete close.
